Graph field guide Wiki graph_field_guide.md castle graph guide Graph field guide castle graph guide Castle builds its relationship graph from the frontmatter of notes in people/. This example library intentionally includes several shapes. What to look for Relation colors: the sample covers positive, neutral, flirty, mixed, and negative connections—from close collaborators to former coworkers. Known from branches: expand Community, Work, Conference, University, and Family. Organizations: Northstar Labs has Research, Design, and Engineering departments; Harbor Commons has Programs and Partnerships. Direct links: dotted connections describe coworkers, friends, family, classmates, and manager relationships. Map locations: several people have coordinates; Jamie demonstrates multiple locations. Follow a cluster Start with Alex, follow the direct edge to Maya, then open Maya's link to Sofia. Their shared notes connect the people graph to the broader knowledge graph through Design principles and the Neighborhood Atlas.

Local-first knowledge Wiki local_first_knowledge.md Local first privacy architecture reference Local-first knowledge Local first privacy architecture reference Local first tools keep the durable source close to the person doing the work. In Castle, Markdown files are authoritative; generated graphs, search indexes, and databases are replaceable views. Practical consequences 1. Notes remain readable without the application. 2. Links such as the research plan remain explicit in source. 3. Sensitive raw interviews can stay outside publishable summaries. 4. A disposable index can make search fast without becoming a second source of truth. Noah applies these ideas to the Atlas data dictionary, especially the consent and evidence fields.

Open studio reflection Journal 2026-09-10_open_studio_reflection.md journal atlas prototype community Open studio reflection 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z journal atlas prototype community The most useful feedback at the [[events/2026/atlas open studio Atlas open studio]] was a request for more uncertainty. Visitors wanted to know whether a place was welcoming for them , not receive a universal verdict. Maya noticed that the large text labels helped people approach the display at their own speed. Sofia suggested carrying that same low pressure feeling into the community listening session. A small revision for the next draft Replace “best places” with “places people return to,” and attach a short reason only when it is shareable. The revision follows [[notes/consent and care the consent guidance]] and gives the team a concrete prompt for interview synthesis.

Field day — harbor to pocket garden Journal 2026-08-27_field_day.md journal fieldwork atlas Field day — harbor to pocket garden 2026-08-27T00:00:00.000Z journal fieldwork atlas Alex, Jamie, and Sofia walked from the harbor steps to the pocket garden using the conversation kit. Illustration of a quiet pocket garden with tall grasses, a curved bench, and a neighborhood path A fictional field day scene. The goal is to notice the conditions for welcome, not to rate a place or its visitors. 09:10 — Harbor steps The strongest signal was not the view but the movable chairs. People made temporary circles, then returned the chairs to the wall. A tiny ritual of care. 10:25 — Bakery window A water bowl and a hand drawn notice created more conversation than the polished signage. This supports the “invite, do not rank” principle in Design principles. 11:40 — Pocket garden There was a genuine quiet corner behind the tall grasses. Sofia noted that the garden feels social without requiring participation—a useful nuance for third place research. Next: synthesize the interviews before the weekly research roundtable.

Consent and care for field notes Notes consent_and_care.md Field-note consent research consent community atlas Consent and care for field notes Field-note consent research consent community atlas The Neighborhood Atlas is a record of invitations, not a directory of people. Every observation should leave someone with more control than they had before the conversation began. Three sharing levels Level What we keep Where it can appear Private Full context and contact details The participant's own follow up only Team summary A paraphrased observation without identifiers Research synthesis Shareable story Participant approved language and attribution Atlas prototype or event display If a participant changes their mind, remove the observation from the next working draft and confirm the change. Do not infer a sharing level from an enthusiastic conversation. Before and after a conversation [ ] Use the conversation kit to explain the purpose. [ ] Ask which sharing level feels right today. [ ] Write observations rather than judgments. [ ] Send a short summary when a follow up route was requested. [ ] Bring any unresolved questions to the community listening session. This is the practical companion to the “invite, do not rank” principle in Design principles.

Design principles Notes design_principles.md Atlas principles design atlas decisions Design principles Atlas principles design atlas decisions true Invite, do not rank The Atlas should help someone participate, not declare which place is “best.” Amara's phrase— a map is an invitation, not an inventory —is the clearest test. Show uncertainty An observation, a recurring pattern, and a hypothesis are different kinds of knowledge. The data dictionary keeps those distinctions visible. Make room for serendipity Useful navigation can be precise without eliminating surprise. Related notes, backlinks, and the graph should reward wandering. Protect the quiet corner Every public activity needs a lower stimulation way to contribute. This is why the open studio task includes a quiet feedback station. Prefer reversible decisions Start with simple Markdown, visible links, and portable files. This follows the logic of Local first knowledge. These principles were reviewed in August studio notes and tested during the field day.

Field-note template Notes field_note_template.md Observation template template research fieldwork Field-note template Observation template template research fieldwork Copy this note after a walk or short conversation. Keep it lightweight enough to use outside, then return to it when you can distinguish what you observed from what you interpreted. Context Place or route: Date and time: Companions: Sharing level: private / team summary / shareable story What happened Describe a small scene: who could enter, what changed the pace, and where someone could choose to pause. Link to a relevant project, person, or event only when that link has the right consent level. Questions to carry forward What would a newcomer need to understand? What should remain unmeasured? Which observation belongs in the next studio conversation? See Consent and care for field notes before sharing the note beyond the immediate team.

Conversation kit Notes interview_kit.md Interview kit Walking interview prompts research interviews template Conversation kit Interview kit Walking interview prompts research interviews template Use these prompts during short walking conversations for the Neighborhood Atlas. Opening Show me a place where you naturally slow down. Ask permission before taking notes. Explain whether the result is private, summarized, or publishable. Prompts What makes this place easy—or difficult—to enter? When does it feel most alive? Is there a ritual a newcomer might not notice? Where is the quiet corner? What would you never want a map to flatten into a rating? Closing checklist [ ] Reflect one thing you heard [ ] Confirm the consent level [ ] Offer a way to revise the summary [ ] Add only the necessary fields to the data dictionary

August studio notes Notes meeting_notes_august.md meeting atlas decisions August studio notes 2026-08-25T00:00:00.000Z meeting atlas decisions Participants: Alex, Jamie, Maya, and Noah. Decisions Use “signals” rather than ratings. Keep consent visible in the working dataset and export. Treat the graph as an exploration surface, not an org chart. Test the prototype at the open studio. Open questions 1. Can a visual legend leave enough room for serendipity? 2. Which parts of the conversation kit are too formal? 3. How should we show disagreement without implying an error? The team agreed to revisit Design principles after the first interview synthesis.

Why third places matter Notes research/third_places.md Third places research community public-space Why third places matter Third places research community public-space “Third places” are informal gathering spaces outside home and work. For the Atlas, the useful idea is not a strict category but a set of qualities: low barriers to entry, regulars and newcomers sharing space, and reasons to linger without a formal appointment. Signals for fieldwork Signal Observation prompt Welcome Can a newcomer understand how to join? Rhythm Are there recurring rituals or familiar faces? Choice Can someone be social or find a quiet corner? Care Is maintenance visible as a shared practice? These signals inform the conversation kit, but they are not scores. That distinction follows Design principles. Related field evidence The field day includes early observations from the harbor steps and pocket garden. Sofia's completed Listening Garden offers another example of a temporary third place.

Welcome to the Neighborhood Atlas Notes welcome.md Start here Demo home castle guide atlas Welcome to the Neighborhood Atlas Start here Demo home castle guide atlas true This publish safe library follows a fictional group building a living guide to their neighborhood. It is deliberately connected: people know one another, projects create tasks and events, journal entries point back to decisions, and the same ideas appear in the Canvas workspace. Start with the Castle feature tour, then open the relationship graph and follow any person or note link that catches your eye. Six good places to begin Explore What it demonstrates Graph field guide Relationship colors, groups, departments, and direct links Neighborhood Atlas A project connected to people, tasks, events, and research Why third places matter A link rich research note with citations and backlinks Field day journal A dated narrative with an original field illustration Consent and care A practical policy note with tasks, events, and follow up links The stash Quick captures for articles, videos, ideas, and loose follow ups The story so far Alex Morgan and Jamie Chen began by mapping the places that make a neighborhood feel welcoming. Maya Singh turned the research into a visual language, while Noah Williams built a lightweight data pipeline. Community hosts Sofia Rossi and Amara Okafor keep the work grounded in real conversations. Their current focus is the Neighborhood Atlas. The earlier Listening Garden is complete, and the Mobile Story Booth is waiting for its next planning window. After the open studio, the group is preparing a community listening session to decide which observations should shape the next public draft. Atlas research plan Projects neighborhood_atlas/research_plan.md research atlas Atlas research plan research atlas Questions 1. Where do people linger without needing to buy something? 2. Which small rituals make a place feel cared for? 3. What information helps a newcomer participate? Method Run eight short walking conversations using the conversation kit. Pair each interview with a sketch, one memorable quote, and a consent level. Jamie leads the interviews, Alex facilitates synthesis, and Maya tests the visual vocabulary. See Data dictionary for the fields and Local first knowledge for why raw interview material stays on the researcher's device.
